frictionVectors.title: EU ENERGY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains substantial control through Sonatrach, but European demand, pricing, and pipeline politics constrain its room for maneuver. LNG and pipeline infrastructure remain tied to external technology and markets.

frictionVectors.title: SOUTHERN SECURITY FRONTIER
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger increases security costs around Algeria's resource-producing south. Algiers resists foreign military involvement while facing pressure to coordinate with competing outside powers.

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Angola has strengthened regulatory control and is seeking investment beyond hydrocarbons, but foreign firms and volatile oil revenues still shape fiscal sovereignty. Declining production limits leverage over external partners.

frictionVectors.title: LOBITO CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Western-backed development of the Lobito Corridor increases Angola's strategic value for copper and cobalt supply chains. Competition with Chinese infrastructure and financing could turn transport access into a source of political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER TRADE DISRUPTION
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger and broader Sahel sanctions politics have disrupted traditional trade routes and exposed Benin's dependence on regional transit networks. Port and pipeline projects remain vulnerable to diplomatic escalation.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Benin is expanding cooperation with regional and external security partners to contain jihadist spillover in the north. Foreign training and maritime support improve capacity but create dependence in critical security infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND MARKET DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured stronger terms in its diamond partnership with De Beers, reinforcing state control over a strategic resource. However, weak global diamond demand and foreign marketing channels remain material vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS INFRASTRUCTURE GAP
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other critical minerals is increasing, but rail, power, and processing constraints limit domestic value capture. External investors may gain disproportionate influence unless beneficiation capacity expands.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD CONTROL STRUGGLE
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state oversight of industrial and artisanal gold, while insecurity and informal networks continue diverting production. Foreign mining capital faces rising regulatory and political uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's turn away from Western security partners toward Russian-linked support has increased political autonomy but not stabilized resource zones. Armed-group activity continues to disrupt roads, mines, and public administration.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Burundi remains highly dependent on external capital and aid while seeking to formalize control over nickel, rare-earth, and gold resources. Limited fiscal and technical capacity weakens the state's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Persistent accusations involving armed groups and cross-border support keep the Burundi-Rwanda frontier politically volatile. Disruption of trade and security cooperation limits regional infrastructure and resource integration.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its ports, airspace, and maritime position to attract European, North American, and Gulf investment. Dependence on outside finance creates exposure to competing strategic agendas around infrastructure ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: Drug trafficking, illegal fishing, and limited surveillance capacity challenge sovereign control across the country's vast maritime zone. External security assistance is valuable but can deepen reliance on foreign actors.

highlights: State retains oil and corridor control

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest regions continues to damage roads, agricultural production, and public authority. The conflict also raises risks for energy and transport projects linking the interior to the Gulf of Guinea.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign partners remain important to major road, port, hydropower, and mining projects. These deals expand infrastructure access but can limit transparency and increase long-term debt and concession pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Bangui relies heavily on Russian-linked security personnel and political backing to protect the regime and key urban corridors. This dependence narrows independent foreign-policy choices and complicates accountability over resource-linked arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Informality
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal mining and conflict-linked smuggling continue to divert gold and diamonds away from formal state revenue channels. Weak transport infrastructure and fragmented territorial control make enforcement and transparent licensing difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon income remains central to state finance, but production volatility and opaque distribution limit broad-based development. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and commercial leverage over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: Chad's strategic position near Libya, Sudan, and the Central African Republic keeps it dependent on external military and diplomatic partnerships. Shifts in European engagement and regional instability increase pressure on sovereign border control and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on foreign financing and contractors for ports, roads, energy, and telecommunications, limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Mayotte dispute continues to strain relations with France, while migration controls and development assistance remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Sovereignty Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-backed investors remain central to cobalt, copper, and coltan production, while weak oversight and opaque contracting constrain the state's ability to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Backed Armed Networks
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to threaten territorial control and mineral corridors in the east, with regional and international actors pursuing competing security agendas.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Financing Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues dominate fiscal capacity, leaving Brazzaville vulnerable to price shocks and limiting policy autonomy when negotiating with external lenders and energy partners.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and industrial projects provide needed connectivity but increase dependence on external finance, contractors, and resource-linked repayment arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Côte d’Ivoire is strengthening domestic processing and pricing institutions, but foreign trading houses and global buyers still capture substantial value from its cocoa economy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in Burkina Faso and Mali are increasing security costs and complicating transport, trade, and infrastructure plans in northern Côte d’Ivoire.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through competing foreign military bases, but the concentration of external security actors constrains independent strategic maneuver and raises sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port revenues and major infrastructure remain closely tied to foreign operators and creditors, particularly China, leaving Djibouti exposed to debt, concession, and regional trade pressures.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and IMF-linked reforms increase reliance on Gulf capital and asset sales, potentially narrowing Cairo's control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and canal security
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and attacks on shipping threaten Suez Canal revenues while Egypt balances relations with Gulf partners, Israel, and major trading powers.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and volatile production leave the state dependent on foreign operators, external markets, and opaque revenue arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Malabo offshore exposure
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas and oil infrastructure remains vulnerable to shifting company commitments and regional maritime competition in the Gulf of Guinea.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia, Sudan, and Red Sea access keep Eritrea exposed to proxy competition and pressure over port usage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide revenue but concentrate strategic influence in a small number of foreign partners amid limited transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Trade and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport corridors, electricity, finance, and market access, limiting room for independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and manufacturing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned agro-industrial and manufacturing interests remain central to exports, while regional trade-rule changes could reduce fiscal and employment stability.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and Red Sea contestation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam improves energy sovereignty but sustains disputes with Egypt and Sudan, while port-access ambitions heighten regional competition.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on Gulf, Chinese, and multilateral financing constrain Addis Ababa's policy space even as domestic power and transport capacity expand.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional-to-electoral authorities are seeking greater national control over oil, manganese, and forestry value chains, creating friction with established French, Chinese, and other foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains dependent on externally financed and managed transport infrastructure to move minerals and timber, limiting its bargaining power despite stronger political control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Weak monitoring capacity leaves Gambian waters vulnerable to illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing by foreign fleets, undermining food security and coastal revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and aid reliance
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on external donors and regional partners for roads, energy, and security support, giving Senegal and international financiers significant influence over strategic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and industrial gold mining, including foreign-linked operations, continues to damage water systems and agricultural land while the state struggles to secure consistent local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is attracting competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf interest in lithium, bauxite, gold, and refining, but fiscal pressures and infrastructure gaps constrain its ability to dictate terms.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external control
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor is dominated by large international consortia and requires foreign-financed rail and port infrastructure, raising concerns over long-term sovereignty and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Junta bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: The military government is using mining licenses and local-processing demands to extract concessions, but political uncertainty and dependence on foreign capital limit its negotiating room.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign traders, price volatility, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime and trafficking risks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited coastal surveillance create openings for narcotics trafficking and illicit maritime activity, increasing the influence of foreign criminal networks and regional security actors.

highlights: Ports and power remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing IMF-backed fiscal reforms against repayment pressure from Chinese and commercial lenders. Strategic transport and energy projects remain vulnerable to foreign financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the northern corridor face competitive pressure from Tanzania and regional alternatives. Gulf, Chinese, and Western actors are all seeking influence over logistics and energy networks.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but deepens dependence on South African financing, infrastructure, and demand. Delays and cost disputes in Phase II could weaken Maseru's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Diamond Sector
frictionVectors.details: Large diamond operations are dominated by foreign capital and exposed to volatile global prices. Local value addition and state participation remain limited.

highlights: Iron ore recovery outpaces local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and Rail Concessions
frictionVectors.details: ArcelorMittal's iron ore operations and associated rail and port access give external investors substantial influence over Liberia's export infrastructure. The government is seeking greater fiscal returns and domestic processing without disrupting production.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Financing
frictionVectors.details: Liberia remains dependent on foreign capital for port modernization and reliable power. Financing terms can constrain procurement choices and long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Oil remains hostage to political fragmentation
Foreign security patrons retain strategic reach

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks can still disrupt production, export terminals, and National Oil Corporation operations. Hydrocarbon revenues remain the central prize in Libya's unresolved power struggle.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, Egypt, and Gulf actors retain influence through military partnerships, contractors, and political clients. Their presence limits unified Libyan control over territory and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Nickel and Cobalt
frictionVectors.details: The Ambatovy complex and other mining operations are dominated by international capital and exposed to global battery-mineral price cycles. Fiscal benefits and local procurement remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Rio Tinto and Community Land Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The QIT Madagascar Minerals operation has generated foreign exchange and infrastructure but continues to face disputes over land, water, compensation, and environmental impacts. Weak enforcement can reduce the state's ability to secure durable local consent.

highlights: Mining expansion tests state bargaining power
Energy and debt pressures narrow policy space

frictionVectors.title: MINING LICENSES AND LOCAL VALUE
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium, rare earths and other minerals while trying to secure stronger local processing and fiscal returns. Limited administrative capacity and external financing needs weaken its negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND FUEL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and reliance on imported fuel expose the country to external price shocks and infrastructure bottlenecks. Regional power links and new generation projects are strategically important but slow to deliver.

highlights: Junta tightens control over gold sector
Sahel sovereignty comes with rising insecurity

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND FOREIGN SECURITY PARTNERS
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating mining terms and asserting greater state control, but security partnerships with Russian-linked actors and other external networks complicate transparency and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: NATIONALIZATION OF REGIONAL ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Withdrawal from regional institutions and deteriorating relations with coastal neighbors increase dependence on constrained transport corridors. Armed-group attacks threaten mines, roads and the state’s ability to secure resource zones.

highlights: Iron and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers new revenue and geopolitical weight, but cross-border management, cost recovery and local-content demands will test Mauritania’s control over the windfall.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron exports and port infrastructure remain dominated by large foreign-linked operators and global commodity cycles. Chinese and Gulf investment can accelerate logistics while increasing concentration risks.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND MARITIME CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to pursue sovereign authority over the Chagos Archipelago while balancing relations with the United Kingdom, United States and India. The issue affects strategic space, fisheries and the country’s diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND FINANCIAL INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Competition among India, China and other partners around port, logistics and digital infrastructure creates opportunities but requires careful safeguards. Mauritius’s dependence on external trade and finance remains its main vulnerability.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the central sovereignty contest

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy and infrastructure projects to consolidate its position in Western Sahara. International legal and diplomatic challenges continue to affect investment risk and relations with Algeria and the European Union.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Renewables, green hydrogen and port expansion increase Morocco’s strategic autonomy, but major projects rely on foreign capital, technology and export markets. Rivalry among European, Gulf, Chinese and U.S. partners requires calibrated alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Gas projects depend on sustained protection around Palma and Afungi, leaving Maputo reliant on foreign security support and multinational operators. Insurgent attacks and local grievances continue to threaten construction and export timelines.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Contract and Revenue Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain substantial influence over project terms, debt structures, and future revenues. The state is seeking greater fiscal benefit while preserving investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Uranium Sovereignty Debate
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil prospects and established uranium operations are increasing pressure for local processing, stronger fiscal terms, and domestic participation. Foreign operators remain central to capital-intensive extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign finance, technology, port access, and export markets. Wind and water constraints create a risk that external investors capture disproportionate value unless domestic linkages improve.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are seeking greater control over uranium and other mineral assets while contesting legacy arrangements with foreign firms. Regulatory uncertainty and diplomatic tension threaten production and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and deeper security cooperation with Russia have changed access, logistics, and intelligence arrangements. Insurgent pressure continues to constrain state control over resource corridors and border regions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Upstream Control
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain important to offshore production, technology, and financing, while the government is trying to expand domestic ownership and capture more value. Contract uncertainty, theft, and regulatory delays continue to weaken bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Power Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and unreliable electricity reduce the state’s effective control over strategic infrastructure. Gas expansion is constrained by financing, security risks, and weak domestic transmission capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Linkages
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda’s regional security posture and mineral-trading networks remain under intense international scrutiny amid conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Sanctions pressure and diplomatic disputes could affect access to markets and foreign support.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Kigali retains strong administrative control but relies on external aid, investment, and security partnerships for parts of its development model. Donor concerns over regional military activity could narrow policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons remain commercially unproven, leaving the country dependent on external firms and licensing expertise. Delays in exploration limit immediate sovereign revenue while raising concerns over contract transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe relies heavily on foreign partners to monitor its extensive maritime zone and protect fisheries and potential energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production strengthens Senegal's bargaining position, but efforts to increase local ownership and revise legacy agreements risk investor disputes and slower project expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and external fleets
frictionVectors.details: Industrial foreign fishing, especially involving distant-water fleets, continues to pressure coastal livelihoods and test Dakar's capacity to enforce resource rules in its maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign access to marine resources
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles uses foreign partnerships and licensing to monetize its large maritime zone, but must balance tuna revenues and investment against conservation and local-control demands.

frictionVectors.title: Security infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Maritime surveillance, port services, and strategic infrastructure require assistance from larger powers, creating exposure to competing Indian Ocean interests.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession leverage
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, diamonds, and other minerals remain central to growth, but foreign operators and concession structures can limit domestic value capture and intensify environmental disputes.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, and energy projects depend substantially on foreign lenders and contractors, increasing debt, procurement, and strategic-dependence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopia-Somaliland access dispute
frictionVectors.details: Competing claims over Somaliland's coastline and potential Ethiopian maritime access directly challenge Mogadishu's territorial sovereignty and invite wider regional intervention.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of ports and security
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, Ethiopia, and other partners provide military, port, and commercial support, but their interests can fragment federal authority and dilute national control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic underperformance at Transnet railways and ports limits South Africa's ability to capture value from coal, iron ore, and critical-mineral exports. Private-sector participation is expanding, but may increase foreign influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL-POLICY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European Union, and China are competing for battery and transition minerals. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation and diversified partnerships while managing investor concerns over regulation and power reliability.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, exposing revenue flows to sabotage, political leverage, and emergency repair costs. Chinese-linked and other foreign operators remain central to production and transport.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE REVENUE FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions, elite patronage, and recurring armed tensions prevent oil income from being converted into broad national development. External financing and security relationships reinforce dependence rather than sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SMUGGLING NETWORKS
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trading routes are contested by armed actors and regional intermediaries, depriving the state of revenue. Gulf-linked markets and alleged external support networks add pressure to Sudan's economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA INFRASTRUCTURE CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and prospective Red Sea facilities have become objects of competition involving Gulf states, Russia, and other outside powers. The conflict makes transport corridors and maritime access strategic bargaining tools.

frictionVectors.title: LNG PROJECT CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Long-delayed offshore LNG negotiations reflect Tanzania's effort to secure stronger fiscal terms, domestic benefits, and regulatory control from international energy firms. Delays preserve bargaining space but defer major infrastructure and export revenue.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital remains essential to large-scale mining, rail, and port development, including projects involving Chinese and Gulf-linked investors. Dar es Salaam is seeking local processing and tighter oversight without deterring investment.

highlights: Lomé port remains a regional hinge

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRADE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo strategic leverage over landlocked Sahelian markets, but its expansion relies heavily on foreign finance, logistics firms, and external shipping networks. Disruptions or sanctions affecting northern corridors could quickly reduce sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in Burkina Faso and the wider Sahel place pressure on Togo's northern border and transport routes. Security cooperation with regional and external partners may improve resilience while increasing dependence on outside support.

highlights: State control tightens as economic autonomy narrows
EU migration and energy leverage remain decisive

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance to perceived external conditionality complicates implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and limited fiscal space, while phosphate production has struggled to recover. These constraints reduce the state's ability to convert strategic resources into sovereign bargaining power.

highlights: Oil infrastructure advances under non-Western financing
Strategic autonomy grows alongside external dependence

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline is backed primarily by Chinese and Gulf-linked capital after Western lenders withdrew or declined participation. Uganda retains political control of the project but accepts significant external financial and market exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Region Land and Environmental Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Land acquisition, displacement, and environmental concerns around oil development continue to generate friction with communities and international advocacy groups. These disputes could delay infrastructure and raise operating costs.

highlights: Copper diplomacy strengthens Zambia's bargaining position
Debt reform opens space for strategic investment

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is attracting competing US, European, Gulf, and Chinese interest in copper and cobalt supply chains. The government is seeking more local processing, but financing and technology gaps limit its leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms improve fiscal credibility while narrowing short-term policy flexibility. Transport, power, and mining infrastructure remain vulnerable to creditor and investor influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain prominent in lithium, platinum, gold, and other mining operations. Export restrictions and beneficiation requirements seek to retain more value domestically but have not overcome financing and processing dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, Finance, and Infrastructure Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Restrictions on access to international finance, governance disputes, and unreliable power infrastructure constrain Zimbabwe's ability to negotiate from strength. Dependence on bilateral lenders and foreign mining capital increases external leverage.
